name: Engine placement: SUMO on server streaming state vs engine in browser (JS or Rust/WASM) vs Python engine behind an API
maintainer: N/A for the decision itself. Components it depends on: Eclipse SUMO (DLR / Eclipse Foundation), hosting providers (Render, Google Cloud Run, Fly.io, Hugging Face, Oracle Cloud), and reference projects (A/B Street, SUMO-Web3D, traffic-simulation.de, UXsim)
first_release: N/A (design decision). Reference points: SUMO-Web3D streaming pattern 2018; A/B Street WASM build about 2020 [uncertain]; SUMO WASM build first proposed as a draft PR in September 2026
last_activity: Evidence checked 2026-11-11: SUMO 1.28.0 wheels on PyPI (eclipse-sumo, libsumo, traci); SUMO WebAssembly PR #18310 still a draft and unmerged (last updated 2026-10-12); Fly.io and Hugging Face free-tier terms as documented in November 2026
licence: Depends on the engine: SUMO EPL-2.0; A/B Street / osm2streets Apache-2.0; UXsim MIT; traffic-simulation.de (movsim) GPL-3.0
language: Server pattern: Python (FastAPI/aiohttp) + libsumo/TraCI (C++ engine). Browser pattern: TypeScript, or Rust compiled to WASM with wasm-pack. API pattern: Python (NumPy-based engine such as UXsim, or custom)
code_availability: All candidate building blocks are open source: SUMO (github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo, pip install eclipse-sumo / libsumo), A/B Street and osm2streets (github.com/a-b-street), UXsim (github.com/toruseo/UXsim), traffic-simulation.de (github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de)
maintenance_health: SUMO is actively maintained with regular releases and binary wheels for Linux x86_64/aarch64, macOS arm64 and Windows, so a server deployment is just a pip install. No maintained SUMO WebAssembly build exists: the only attempt is an AI-generated draft PR (#18310, September 2026) whose author has not yet signed the Eclipse contributor agreement. In-browser engines are therefore custom code you maintain yourself.
network_import: Server/SUMO: OSM -> netconvert (or osmWebWizard) -> .net.xml on the server; edits mean regenerating the network server-side. Browser: OSM (Overpass XML) -> osm2streets-js (WASM) or a custom TS parser in the client, with no server round-trip. Python API: OSM -> osmnx/custom importer on the server, or a pre-baked JSON network shipped with the app.
demand_input_formats: Server/SUMO: SUMO route/flow XML (generate from UI parameters with randomTrips or flow definitions). Browser and Python: our own JSON scenario (origin-destination flows per vehicle class per hour), which is simplest and keeps the UI schema identical across engine choices.
data_access: N/A for the decision; OSM extracts via Overpass/Geofabrik (ODbL).
runs_in_browser_or_server: Pattern A (SUMO on server, streaming): engine on server, browser renders. Pattern B (engine in browser): everything client-side, server only serves static files. Pattern C (Python engine behind API): engine on server, either batch (run, then return results/trajectories) or streaming.
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: SUMO cannot realistically run in the browser in 72 hours: no official WASM build exists, only a draft, unmerged, AI-generated libsumo-to-WebAssembly PR (#18310). SUMO must therefore stream from a server (proven by SUMO-Web3D: TraCI -> frame diffs -> WebSocket -> three.js). Custom engines in JS or Rust/WASM are proven in the browser: A/B Street runs its full simulator as WASM at play.abstreet.org, traffic-simulation.de runs IDM/MOBIL microsimulation in plain JavaScript, and alexose/traffic-visualizer runs a Rust/WASM IDM engine with WebGL2. Python engines can run in the browser via Pyodide, but that was not verified here for any traffic simulator [uncertain].
api: Pattern A: libsumo (in-process, fastest, single simulation per process; 'cannot be used to connect multiple clients') or TraCI over a socket (slower; multiple clients possible); the web server exposes REST to create/edit a scenario and a WebSocket for frames. Pattern B: a JS/WASM module interface (e.g. sim.tick(dt), sim.positions() -> Float32Array), so no network API is needed. Pattern C: REST POST /scenarios -> job id; GET /results; optional WebSocket for frames.
performance: SUMO TraCI reference (Bologna, 9,000 vehicles, 5,000 steps): about 8 s plain SUMO, about 42 s with TraCI subscriptions, about 90 s with naive per-vehicle Python queries, so state extraction, not simulation, is the bottleneck in Pattern A; libsumo removes the socket overhead. UXsim (pure-Python mesoscopic): about 60,000 vehicles over a 2-hour, 10 km x 10 km grid in about 30 s on a desktop (under 1 s in its optional C++ mode), so a Python meso engine is viable for batch runs but not for per-vehicle 2D lateral microsimulation at scale. Browser: no shared benchmark; A/B Street notes its single WASM bundle 'didn't scale' and was split per city [uncertain for vehicle counts]. Network latency: Pattern B has none per frame; Patterns A and C add one RTT per frame or per result plus serialisation; with India-to-US/EU free-tier regions expect roughly 150-300 ms RTT [uncertain], acceptable for buffered playback but not for tight interaction.
gpu_requirement: None for any pattern (CPU simulation). The browser renderer needs WebGL/WebGL2 for thousands of agents.
multi_tenancy_model: Pattern A: libsumo allows one simulation per process, and parallel runs need Python multiprocessing, so N concurrent users mean N SUMO processes (tens to hundreds of MB each [uncertain]). On a 512 MB free instance [uncertain] that caps concurrency at a few users; you need a job queue (one worker, others wait) or session-to-process mapping, and every open WebSocket keeps a Cloud Run instance 'active' and billed. Pattern B: client-side, so each user's CPU runs their own simulation and the marginal server cost is about zero (static CDN), which scales to any number of users. Pattern C: a shared Python process can run several scenarios if the engine is reentrant (plain objects, no globals), but the GIL means one core per process; batch-run-then-return fits free tiers better than long-lived streams.
build_complexity: Pattern A: low engine effort (pip install eclipse-sumo libsumo; Docker image with SUMO), moderate glue (process pool, cleanup, WebSocket diffing, netconvert on edits); SUMO's lane-based model needs the sublane model configured for Indian traffic. Pattern B: highest engine effort (write or port the model in TS or Rust), lowest ops effort (static hosting on GitHub Pages / Cloudflare Pages / Netlify / Vercel); Rust/WASM adds a wasm-pack toolchain and JS<->WASM boundary design, while plain TypeScript is fastest to iterate in 72 hours. Pattern C: moderate (FastAPI + custom or UXsim engine; Docker; job runner); simplest to debug.
scenario_editability: Pattern A: edits (lane count, width, signals) need regenerating the SUMO network (netconvert / XML patch) and restarting the simulation, giving a slower edit loop. Pattern B: edit in-memory objects and restart instantly, the best fit for 'tweak and rerun'. Pattern C: same as B, plus an HTTP round-trip.
output_metrics_supported: Pattern A: SUMO's built-in outputs (tripinfo, edgeData, queue output, emissions) for free. Patterns B and C: only what we implement (travel time, delay, queue length, throughput are cheap; emissions and conflicts are not).
emissions_support: Pattern A gets SUMO's HBEFA-based emission models for free; Patterns B and C must implement their own (e.g. a simple speed-based factor table) or skip.
known_limitations: Pattern A: process-per-simulation (libsumo), cold starts (Render free spins down after 15 min idle, about 1 min to wake), a 750 instance-hours/month cap, ephemeral filesystem, Cloud Run WebSocket max 60-minute timeout with best-effort session affinity, Hugging Face Docker Spaces now require a paid plan (only static Spaces are free), Fly.io has no free tier for new organisations (only $1 trial credit; bills under $5/month waived), and SUMO lane-based defaults need sublane configuration for Indian traffic. Pattern B: the engine must be written from scratch, performance depends on the user's device (low-end phones), there are no built-in validated models, and all scenario data is client-visible. Pattern C: the Python GIL, slower per-agent loops, and the same cold-start and free-tier caps as A.
documented_failures: A/B Street: a monolithic WASM bundle 'didn't scale' and detangling native-only dependencies for the web was 'quite tough'. SUMO-Web3D: the server-streaming viewer was archived after 2018 and never tracked SUMO releases. SUMO TraCI docs: naive per-vehicle polling is about 11x slower than plain SUMO in the Bologna benchmark. The SUMO WASM attempt (PR #18310) is stalled as a draft on contributor-agreement paperwork.
validation_approach: Evidence from primary documentation (SUMO Libsumo and TraCI docs with the Bologna timing table; Render, Cloud Run, Fly.io, Hugging Face and Oracle free-tier docs), working public deployments (play.abstreet.org WASM, traffic-simulation.de JS), and repository inspection (SUMO-Web3D architecture, traffic-visualizer WASM exports, SUMO PR #18310 status).
takeaway_for_our_build: Recommended for 72 hours and free hosting: Pattern B (engine in the browser, written in TypeScript, optionally later ported to Rust/WASM), deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages / Cloudflare Pages / Netlify. It is the only option that is truly free at any user count, has no cold starts, no per-user processes and no WebSocket billing, and suits a custom Indian mixed-traffic (non-lane, 2D lateral) model that SUMO does not provide out of the box anyway. Run the simulation in a Web Worker, exchange positions as Float32Array (transferable), render with deck.gl or WebGL instancing, and keep the scenario as JSON so the engine is swappable. Keep a scoped Pattern A as a stretch or validation path: a FastAPI + libsumo Docker service on a free VM (Oracle Always Free Ampere A1 gives 2 OCPU / 12 GB but reclaims idle instances) or Render free (sleeps, 750 h/month), run as batch jobs with a single-worker queue rather than live streams, used to cross-check our engine on one junction. Avoid planning on Hugging Face Docker Spaces or Fly.io as free hosts (both now need payment), and avoid relying on SUMO-in-WASM (draft only). Design rules: (1) one engine interface (load(scenario), step(dt), snapshot()) so A, B or C can sit behind it; (2) send only viewport-visible agents, as typed arrays; (3) cap scenario size (e.g. under 5,000 agents and one corridor) so it runs on mid-range phones [uncertain threshold]; (4) precompute OSM imports offline and ship JSON, because live Overpass imports are a demo-day failure risk.
